doc.title: Dave Bailey and John McNeil Interview, 1959-10-25

title: Disliking crowds and outplaying a rival drummer in a church parade
summary: Bailey says he never followed parades and hates crowds, then tells how he tied another band in knots with his drumming.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: Well when you were a kid, did you follow any drummers around or anything?

Never just follow no parades when I was a kid. Never follow no parades around. Just go and look at them. See on Conville Day, hardly go and see Conville parades. I don't like to be in the monster gang of people. Never do. Can't stand to be amongst the crowd. Right now, when I'm working now at the hospital, the crowd go up on the elevator, I let them go up and I catch the next elevator. I never liked it from a kid up, never liked to be in the crowd. I used to go to theaters. Sometimes they had the, when they had the regular theaters like Chris and all them theaters. What'd I do? All these 50 shows? If you beat you amongst the crowd, I'll come back home. Never liked to be in the crowd, that's the fact. I don't even ride a crowded bus. Busy crowd, I won't get on. I'd rather be late going to work and get on crowded. But I don't know if this, don't like it. Don't like to be in the crowd. So it's all right as long as I know they don't try to buck against me, you see. If they go to work and try to buck, then I'm a couple of them. I beat a part playing during this church, we played at this church over here twice. I played in the Jackson band then. You know Kid Howell? It was his band. And you know this brother called Brother Conberry, played climate. He was playing with them. Pajo, all that was a band. He had a short duffer you know. I didn't have this set of drums, the other drums, but that big 28. I'll give it to a friend of mine. I let him out of that room too small. And the band, see we was the last band. The band, the first band, they were supposed to stop playing. The last band come up with the crew. After we come up with our crew they just kept on playing, pull on the side and kept on playing. I told the boy, I said don't stop playing, let's keep on playing. And I cut loose on that drum there. It was too bad. And when he tried to make what I'd make and I'd make different beats, I got him all kind of it. And he said, I told you you can't play no drums with that man. You just can't beat him. You've been playing since he was a little kid. You can't do it with him. That's a gift. And they all come in shaking hands with me. And when I was little, he called me, the boy about 12 or 13 years old, went up there and told my laddie, he said, Miss Margaret, Mr. Dave tied that band all up in the knot. He said, the band hadn't stopped playing. The band was trying to buck in and say, Mr. Dave cut loose on that drum and tied the whole drum. Everybody laughed. And the man that played so much drum, the man took me around the corner. And I said, come on boys, go with me. I got to give you something to drink. He carried the drum, brought me to his house. He had beer, he had home, I know what all that that band had in his place. Yeah. You want some whiskey? I know. You're the best drummer I've ever seen in this city.
